chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Ash'ari, from Ibn al-Qaddah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) said: 'The exception (istithna') in an oath is valid whenever it is remembered, even if it is after forty mornings.'
Then he recited this Verse: 'And remember your Lord when you forget.'

key_terms.أَرْبَعِينَ صَبَاحاً: Forty mornings (a specific time period in jurisprudence)
key_terms.الِاسْتِثْنَاءُ: Exception or reservation of a condition in an oath

ai.seo_question: How long does an exception (istithna) remain valid in an Islamic oath if forgotten?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies that the validity of 'istithna' (exception) in an oath is not bound by a strict time limit, remaining effective as long as the oath-taker remembers it, even after forty mornings. By citing the verse 'And remember your Lord when you forget' (18:24), Imam al-Sadiq (AS) links the legal mechanism of memory to the Quranic concept of divine facilitation for those who err. This reflects the Shia juristic principle that ease and flexibility are prioritized in fulfilling vows, provided the intention to fulfill or exempt is maintained through remembrance.
